extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; general educated readers interested in poetic criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A lecture-style critical account of what makes poetry (and poets) effective, illustrated via major authors (Homer, the Bible, Dante, Ossian, Chaucer, Spenser). Gives evaluative principles and illustrative examples for judging poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and natural sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should excite a voluntary, immediate sympathy in the reader rather than a forced, contrived feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts Richardson (whose interest is "worked up" by innumerable little contrivances) with true poetry: "The sympathy excited is not a voluntary contribution, but a tax." Good poetry makes the reader's heart answer spontaneously ("The heart does not answer of itself like a chord in music" is a fault). Avoid reliance on artificial devices that coerce emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elasticity and forward motion of the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination should run ahead of the writer with momentum and expectation; poetry needs elasticity and motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of "elasticity and motion" means the fancy is "dragged along with an infinite number of pins and wheels." The author uses metaphors (Ariel confined in a pine-tree) to show that poetical genius must not require an "artificial process" to be released. Poems should move naturally, not be mechanically contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs. eloquence (instantaneous sympathy over argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is the eloquence of the imagination that produces instantaneous sympathy; eloquence proper persuades the will and convinces the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction: "Eloquence tries to persuade the will, and convince the reason: poetry produces its effect by instantaneous sympathy." Consequently, subjects that admit of dispute (i.e., argumentative/didactic matters) are ill-suited to poetry. Poetry aims at sympathy and imagination rather than debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate subject-matter (natural, not abstruse or didactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects for poetry should be natural and capable of imaginative sympathy; abstruse, dry, or overly didactic subjects are poor material for poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: Burke's writings, despite vivid fancy, are not poetry because their subject-matter is "abstruse and dry, not natural, but artificial." The French tendency to be "didactic more than dramatic" is criticized. Avoid selecting topics that inherently invite dispute or abstract argument when writing poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere poetic diction or ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must not be only 'poetry in the rhyme' or dependent on studied poetic diction; form must arise from imaginative content, not stylistic artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes some admired poetry that is merely poetic in diction. French poetry is noted for lacking the 'forms of the imagination' and being overly didactic. Poetic language should flow from imaginative necessity rather than be an outer ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeric qualities: action, vigour, and multitudinous form
rubrics_metrics.description: Homeric poetry is dominated by action and life: bright, strong, full of numbers and formal splendour; it depicts bodies as well as souls and organizes large scenes vividly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer's principle of action yields prodigality of life: heroes described "all plumed... covered with glittering armour, with dust and blood," with gods mingling in the fray. The poetry is of number and form, bringing together many countries, manners, and a magnificent multitude of things (splendour, truth, force, variety). Use of vivid, large-scale pictorial description is a Homeric virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biblical qualities: imagination, faith, and immensity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bible's poetry is of imagination and faith: abstract, vast, unformed, and infinite; it aggrandizes into unity and evokes providence and solitude rather than social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This poetry is 'not of form, but of power; not of multitude, but of immensity.' Imagery (e.g., Book of Job) can be more prodigal and intense than Homer. Biblical metaphors are bold and collectivizing, presenting nature and God as immense and omnipresent, and emphasizing the visionary and eternal rather than strong pictorial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dantean qualities: power, passion, and internalized imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Dante's poetry is the poetry of power, passion, and self-will; his imagination imparts its own force to objects, combining intense inner feeling with external images to create an overwhelming effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dante is described as 'the sullen heat of a furnace' whose poetry bears a 'gloomy abstraction' and 'a benumbing stupor' yet never flags because of the author's continuous earnestness. He often uses few large pictorial subjects but makes the mind 'lend its own power to the objects' (objects gain grandeur through the poet's character). He unites the local and individual with wild mysticism, sometimes heightening effect by bold intermixture of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ossianic qualities: melancholy, decay, and sense of loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Ossianic poetry conveys decay, old age, and a pervasive sense of privation: loss of friends, country, and even God; an atmosphere of cheerless desolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ossian 'lives only in the recollection and regret of the past' and evokes images like 'the cold moonlight... the fox peeps out of the ruined tower' and the harp's strings 'to sigh and rustle like the dry reeds in the winter's wind.' The lamentation for lost things (e.g., Selma for Salgar) is a high achievement in this mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity, truthfulness, and natural simplicity (Chaucerian ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should aim for truth and naturalness: describing persons and things with the accuracy and discrimination of an eyewitness; simplicity and sincerity rather than affected display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer is praised for speaking 'of what he wishes to describe with the accuracy... of one who relates what has happened to himself.' His beauty and pathos 'are not of the poet's seeking' but part of the fable's texture. The poet should find 'grace and beauty in truth' and avoid artificial pomp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony of materials and focus on essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetry economizes its material: it refrains from pompous display, keeps metaphors few and functional, and dwells on essentials rather than ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer exhibits a 'strict parsimony of the poet's materials'—he 'exhibits the naked object, with little drapery.' Metaphors are 'few' and used 'as like as possible to the things themselves.' The effect is directness and tangible accuracy rather than flamboyant embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picturesque-dramatic blending and symbolic description
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions should be both picturesque and dramatic, using external appearances (dress, costume, equipage) as symbols that indicate internal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer's pilgrims (the Knight, the Wife of Bath, the Prioresse, the Monk, the Sompnoure, etc.) are examples where costume and external detail 'speak for themselves.' The picturesque and dramatic are 'closely blended'—external markers signal inner traits and social types (Chaucer 'numbered the classes of men').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangible, sensorial description (effect of sculpture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic description ought to have a tangible, sensorial quality that gives the mental effect of sculpture—concrete sensations of air, ground, coolness, scent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer's natural scenery ('Flower and the Leaf') is praised for local truth and freshness that conveys 'the very feeling of the air, the coolness or moisture of the ground.' Such tangible particulars make inanimate objects share the story's feeling and render the scene believable and affecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minuteness and faithful particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful attention to small, material circumstances (minute realism) strengthens credibility and interest; the narrative chain is built of many fine, connected links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer's minute details—e.g., Palamon left alone in his cell, 'the pure fetters on his shinnes grete / Were of his bitter sake teres wete'—are evidence of fidelity that can sometimes be prolix but is not mere diffuseness. This minute realism grounds emotion and character in concrete fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of variety vs diffuseness
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may be prolix by touching many material points without being diffuse in any single one; variety of linked details should not devolve into pointless digression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaucer is noted as 'prolix from the number of points on which he touches, without being diffuse on any one'—the chain of story consists of 'fine links, closely connected together.' The poet should maintain narrative cohesion while admitting multiplicity of truthful particulars.
